newsitem.title: USA: Asbestos ruling seen reinforcing Congress' role.
newsitem.headline: Asbestos ruling seen reinforcing Congress' role.

text.p: A U.S. Supreme Court ruling throwing out an asbestos settlement appeared to reinforce the view that last week's proposed landmark tobacco deal and other large class-action cases should be resolved through Congress, legal experts said.
The legal experts said the ruling was discouraging for people who have been exposed to a harmful substance but were not injured and hoped to be part of a future settlement through the courts.
"It basically suggests that someone in that situation either will have to get some legislative resolution or wait until they get hurt," Harvard Law Professor Laurence Tribe said.

The experts said the asbestos and tobacco cases were not clearly linked -- the asbestos litigation involved a proposed court settlement under federal rules and the tobacco deal would become effective through legislation Congress must approve and the President must sign.

One legal expert said Wednesday's asbestos ruling did not have a direct impact on the proposed tobacco settlement because the justices did not base their decision on a constitutional prohibition on limiting future tort claimants.

"Because the tobacco settlement has to go through Congress in any event, the limitations that the Supreme Court spoke to in the asbestos case is inapplicable," Florida University Law Professor Lars Noah said.

The Supreme Court upheld a U.S. Appeals Court ruling that threw out a $1.3 billion settlement between 20 former asbestos manufacturers and about 100,000 people claiming injuries from the once widely used substance.
The justices voted 6-2 in ruling that the interests of the various plaintiffs were too diverse and too much in conflict to meet the class-action lawsuit definition under federal court rules.
The case had been closely watched because of its possible implications for the $368.5 billion settlement announced last week between the tobacco industry and U.S. states.

"Philosophically, the court said that massive class settlement procedures might be just a great social idea but they're not within the purview of the courts under the rules," Law Professor John Jacobi of Seton Hall University in Newark, New Jersey, said. "Less philosophically, the court is saying the rule requires that there be adequate representation of the entire class."
In her majority ruling, Justice Ruth Bader Ginsburg pointedly noted that Congress had not adopted a nationwide claims processing system to compensate victims of asbestos exposure.

"Nothing that the court said cast a shadow on the authority of Congress to achieve a nationwide resolution," said Tribe of Harvard University. "In fact, in three points in the court's resolution, it goes out of its way to talk about how this case, the asbestos case, involves the circumstance that one confronts in the face of legislative inaction."

He said Wednesday's decision encourages Congress to pass legislation, although policy issues remained -- for example, whether the state attorneys general who negotiated the tobacco deal were able to extract enough from the tobacco industry in terms of the authority of the Federal Drug Administration.
